knowledge_point.title: Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[1,2]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+y-xy-3 \\ {x}^{2}-x+y-2\end{bmatrix}. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,0]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[2,\,1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).

{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+y-xy-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+y-xy-3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-x+y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-x+y-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x-y & 1-x \\ 2x-1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x-y & 1-x \\ 2x-1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+y-xy-3 \\ {x}^{2}-x+y-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x-y & 1-x \\ 2x-1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+y-xy-3 \\ {x}^{2}-x+y-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(2)-(1) & 1-(2) \\ 2(2)-1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(2)^{2}+(1)-(2)(1)-3 \\ (2)^{2}-(2)+(1)-2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{11}{6} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}1.833 \\ 0.5\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

knowledge_point.title: Computing Second-Order Derivatives

question.:question/problem:
Given the function $f(x, y, z) = x^{2}y + yz^{2}$, compute $∇_{x, y}(∇_{x, y}f)$.
$∇_{x, y}(∇_{x, y}f) =$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the variable subset gradient:

$$
\nabla_{x,y}f=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^{2}y+yz^{2}) \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^{2}y+yz^{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2xy \\ x^{2}+z^{2}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Next, we compute the second derivatives with respect to $x$ and $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(2xy) &=2y & \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2xy) &=2x \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^{2}+z^{2}) &=2x & \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^{2}+z^{2}) &=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla_{x,y}(\nabla_{x,y}f) &=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}} & \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x\partial y} \\ \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y\partial x} & \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x \\ 2x & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}+x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}+x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-{y}^{4}-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-{y}^{4}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{3}+1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & -4{y}^{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{3}+1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & -4{y}^{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}+x \\ {x}^{3}-{y}^{4}-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{3}+1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2y \\ 3{x}^{2} & -4{y}^{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}+x \\ {x}^{3}-{y}^{4}-2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(2)(-1)^{3}+1 & 3(2)^{2}(-1)^{2}-2(-1) \\ 3(2)^{2} & -4(-1)^{3}\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(2)^{2}(-1)^{3}-(-1)^{2}+2 \\ (2)^{3}-(-1)^{4}-2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 14 \\ 12 & 4\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-3)\cdot 4-14\cdot 12}\begin{bmatrix}4 & -14 \\ -12 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{180}\begin{bmatrix}-82 \\ 21\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{139}{90} \\ -\frac{53}{60}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}1.544 \\ -0.883\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-25) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-25) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y-20) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y-20)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2y \\ 2x & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2y \\ 2x & -1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-25 \\ {x}^{2}-y-20\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2y \\ 2x & -1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-25 \\ {x}^{2}-y-20\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(5) & 2(5) \\ 2(5) & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(5)^{2}+(5)^{2}-25 \\ (5)^{2}-5-20\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}10 & 10 \\ 10 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}25 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{10\cdot (-1)-10\cdot 10}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -10 \\ -10 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}25 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{110}\begin{bmatrix}-25 \\ -250\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{105}{22} \\ \frac{30}{11}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}4.773 \\ 2.727\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [1,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}+2xy-3x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,2]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}≈$
$0.375$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}+2xy-3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}+2xy-3x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6xy-2x+2y-3 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy-2x+2y-3) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy-2x+2y-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6y-2 & 6x+2 \\ 6x+2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}6y-2 & 6x+2 \\ 6x+2 & 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}6xy-2x+2y-3 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}6y-2 & 6x+2 \\ 6x+2 & 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}6xy-2x+2y-3 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6(2)-2 & 6(1)+2 \\ 6(1)+2 & 0\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}6(1)(2)-2(1)+2(2)-3 \\ 3(1)^{2}+2(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}10 & 8 \\ 8 & 0\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{10\cdot 0-8\cdot 8}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -8 \\ -8 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{64}\begin{bmatrix}-40 \\ -38\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.375 \\ 1.406\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8xy+2x \\ 4{x}^{2}+2y-5\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy+2x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}+2y-5) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy+2x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}+2y-5)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8y+2 & 8x \\ 8x & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y+2 & 8x \\ 8x & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy+2x \\ 4{x}^{2}+2y-5\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y+2 & 8x \\ 8x & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy+2x \\ 4{x}^{2}+2y-5\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.2 \\ -0.3\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}8(-0.3)+2 & 8(1.2) \\ 8(1.2) & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}8(1.2)(-0.3)+2(1.2) \\ 4(1.2)^{2}+2(-0.3)-5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.2 \\ -0.3\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-0.4 & 9.6 \\ 9.6 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-0.48 \\ 0.16\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.2 \\ -0.3\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-0.4)\cdot 2-(9.6)\cdot (9.6)}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -9.6 \\ -9.6 & -0.4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-0.48 \\ 0.16\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.2 \\ -0.3\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{92.96}\begin{bmatrix}-2.496 \\ 4.544\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}1.173 \\ -0.251\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$-0.07$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}-2{x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}-8) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}-2{x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}-8)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4x+{y}^{2} \\ 2xy+10y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x+{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+10y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x+{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+10y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2y \\ 2y & 2x+10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2y \\ 2y & 2x+10\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}-4x+{y}^{2} \\ 2xy+10y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2y \\ 2y & 2x+10\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}-4x+{y}^{2} \\ 2xy+10y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1.4 \\ 0.4\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 2(0.4) \\ 2(0.4) & 2(-1.4)+10\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-4(-1.4)+(0.4)^{2} \\ 2(-1.4)(0.4)+10(0.4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1.4 \\ 0.4\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & 7.2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}5.76 \\ 2.88\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1.4 \\ 0.4\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-4)\cdot (7.2)-(0.8)\cdot (0.8)}\begin{bmatrix}7.2 & -0.8 \\ -0.8 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5.76 \\ 2.88\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1.4 \\ 0.4\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{29.44}\begin{bmatrix}39.168 \\ -16.128\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-0.07 \\ -0.148\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)-6y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=5x(t)+{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$\,\,u,\,$
where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\boldsymbol{f}(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-6y \\ 5x+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-6y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-6y)=-6 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x+{y}^{2})=5,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5x+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & -6 \\ 5 & 2y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(0) & -6 \\ 5 & 2(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 5 & 0\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Linear Approximations Near Equilibria

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)-2x(t)+3y(t)+3 \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-4x(t)+2{y}^{2}(t)-y(t)+5\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[2,\text{ }-1]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$\,\,u,\,$
where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\boldsymbol{f}(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and 
$$
\displaystyle \boldsymbol{f}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}-2x+3y+3 \\ -4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+3y+3)=2x-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+3y+3)=3 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5)=-4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x+2{y}^{2}-y+5)=4y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x-2 & 3 \\ -4 & 4y-1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(2)-2 & 3 \\ -4 & 4(-1)-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ -4 & -5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ -4 & -5\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

question.:question/problem:

${∇}_{a,b}\,f=\text{ }$

{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute ${∇}_{a,b}\,f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to $a$ and $b.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂a} & =\frac{∂}{∂a}(a{x}^{2}+bx)={x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂b} & =\frac{∂}{∂b}(a{x}^{2}+bx)=x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{a,b}\,f & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂a} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂b}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2} \\ x\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:

{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we take the variable subset gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x,y}\,f & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{yz}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{yz})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{yz} \\ xz{e}^{yz}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the second derivatives with respect to $x$ and $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{yz})=0\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{yz})=z{e}^{yz} \\  & \frac{∂}{∂x}(xz{e}^{yz})=z{e}^{yz}\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂y}(xz{e}^{yz})=x{z}^{2}{e}^{yz}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x,y}({∇}_{x,y}\,f) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & z{e}^{yz} \\ z{e}^{yz} & x{z}^{2}{e}^{yz}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[2,3]\times [1,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-6y+13. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[3,\,2]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[2.25,\,1.5]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{2}≈$
{{field-1}}
$1.417$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-6y+13) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{y}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-6y+13)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-6x \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-6x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-6) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-6x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6x-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}6x-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-6x \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}6x-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}-6x \\ 3{y}^{2}-6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}6(2.25)-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6(1.5)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3(2.25)^{2}-6(2.25) \\ 3(1.5)^{2}-6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}7.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1.6875 \\ 0.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{7.5\cdot 9-0\cdot 0}\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 7.5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.6875 \\ 0.75\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2.25 \\ 1.5\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{67.5}\begin{bmatrix}15.1875 \\ 5.625\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}2.025 \\ 1.417\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing One Iteration of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,0]\times [-2,0]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,-1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}≈$
$-0.444$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-xy-2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8xy+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}-x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy+6x-y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}-x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8y+6 & 8x-1 \\ 8x-1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y+6 & 8x-1 \\ 8x-1 & 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y+6 & 8x-1 \\ 8x-1 & 0\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy+6x-y-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}8(-1)+6 & 8(-1)-1 \\ 8(-1)-1 & 0\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}8(-1)(-1)+6(-1)-(-1)-2 \\ 4(-1)^{2}-(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -9 \\ -9 & 0\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-2)\cdot 0-(-9)\cdot (-9)}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 9 \\ 9 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{81}\begin{bmatrix}45 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-0.444 \\ -1.012\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$
